references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew: "But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven" ([ref:Matt 10:33|Matthew 10:33]). Jesus gives the same warning in the context of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew, with the difference that Matthew says "before my Father who is in heaven" while Luke says "before God's angels."

Jesus says: "For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" ([ref:Mark 8:38|Mark 8:38]). This expresses the same principle that denying Jesus leads to him denying that person at judgment.

The immediately preceding verse, where Jesus promises that whoever confesses him before men, the Son of Man will also acknowledge before God's angels ([ref:Luk 12:8|Luke 12:8]). Verse 9 is the negative counterpart to this promise.

Paul writes: "If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he will also deny us" ([ref:2 Tim 2:12|2 Timothy 2:12]). This directly reflects Jesus' words that denying him results in mutual denial.

Peter's denial of Jesus is a concrete example of denying Christ before men ([ref:Joh 18:25-27|John 18:25-27]). Peter denied three times that he knew Jesus, illustrating the seriousness of Jesus' warning.
Peter warns against false teachers who "deny the Master who bought them" ([ref:2 Pet 2:1|2 Peter 2:1]). Denying the Lord brings destruction upon oneself, in line with Jesus' warning in Luke 12:9.
Jude warns against ungodly people who "deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ" ([ref:Jud 1:4|Jude 1:4]). Denial of Christ is a mark of those destined for judgment.

Jesus says: "I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness!" ([ref:Matt 7:23|Matthew 7:23]). This shows that at judgment Jesus will reject those who do not truly belong to him, which corresponds to being denied before God's angels.
